News / Stock Story / Deere earnings: What to look for

Deere earnings: What to look for 1 min read

DE

Agricultural and construction machinery company Deere DE will be reporting results this Wednesday morning. Here’s what to look for. Deere beat analysts’ revenue expectations last quarter, reporting revenues of $12.61 billion, up 4.9% year on year. It was a solid quarter for the company, with a beat of analysts’ EPS estimates. Is Deere a buy or sell going into earnings? Read our full analysis here, it’s free for active Edge members . This quarter, the market is expecting Deere’s revenue to decline 2.7% year on year, a reversal from the 11.2% increase it recorded in the same quarter last year.

Analysts covering the company have generally reconfirmed their estimates over the last 30 days, suggesting they anticipate the business will stay the course heading into earnings. Deere rarely misses Wall Street’s revenue estimates. Looking at Deere’s peers in the agricultural machinery segment, some have already reported their Q3 results, giving us a hint as to what we can expect. Lindsay delivered year-on-year revenue growth of 5.2%, beating analysts’ expectations by 7.3%, and AGCO reported a revenue decline of 8.6%, falling short of estimates by 2.7%. Lindsay’s stock price was unchanged after the resultswhile AGCO was up 8.6%. Read our full analysis of Lindsay’s results here and AGCO’s results here . In the last year or so, investors have shifted their focus from one macro dynamic to the next (AI disintermediation and AI investment to geopolitical conflict, interest rates, and the health of the wider economy). While some of the agricultural machinery stocks have shown solid performance in this choppy environment, the group has generally underperformed, with share prices down 2.8% on average over the last month. Deere’s stock price was unchanged during the same time and is heading into earnings with an average analyst price target of $694.01 (compared to the current share price of $636.00). ALSO WORTH WATCHING: Nvidia’s Quiet Partner. Nvidia’s chips cost a hundred grand. The connectors that make them work cost even more. One company makes them all. Every AI server needs specialized infrastructure the chip companies don’t make. High-speed cables. Power connectors. Thermal sensors. This 90-year-old company built a monopoly on it. The AI boom just started. This stock is still flying under the radar.

item.content:encoded:
News / Crypto Briefing / Chainalysis traces billions stolen in Binance hack with its new AI tool

Chainalysis traces billions stolen in Binance hack with its new AI tool 2 min read

BNBUSD Chainalysis says its new AI investigation tool helped trace billions of dollars in crypto stolen from Binance. The funds moved across nearly a dozen blockchains. The heist drained approximately $6.4 billion from Binance's hot wallets on October 29, 2026. That makes it the largest single theft the crypto sector has recorded. The attackers moved fast, and the investigators needed to move faster. The attack began at 4:20 p.m. ET. Most of the money left Binance within a roughly 20-minute window. Chainalysis ran its investigation using Chain, an AI-native workspace the firm built for blockchain investigators. The analysis pointed to TraderTraitor, a hacking group linked to North Korea. The attribution rests on on-chain evidence. Stolen Binance funds were commingled with proceeds from an earlier exploit of Bitget in September 2026, just weeks before. Mixing loot from two jobs is efficient for the thieves. It also leaves a fingerprint. The laundering playbook was described as unprecedented. It involved thousands of recursive transactions, with funds cycled rapidly through a long chain of blockchain addresses. One oddly specific detail stood out. Many of those transaction sequences started with exactly 1 TRX on the Tron blockchain. Exchanges and stablecoin issuers moved to lock down what they could. As of early November 2026, approximately $2.8 billion had been frozen through that coordinated effort. Binance estimated the frozen total could reach as high as $3 billion. The hackers clearly understood how freezes work. Stablecoins like USDT and USDC have issuers that can blacklist addresses and lock tokens in place. Ether has no such central switch. So the attackers swapped around $325 million in stablecoins for about $285 million in ETH, and they did it in roughly 20 minutes. They accepted a noticeably worse rate to get out of assets that could be frozen. Chainalysis publicly launched Chain on November 19, 2026. The company pointed to the Binance investigation as a showcase for what the tool can do. The firm is pitching Chain on real-time monitoring and automated workflows. The idea is to let investigators follow illicit funds across different blockchains without manually stitching together each hop. TraderTraitor's alleged involvement fits a pattern that investigators have flagged before. North Korea-linked groups have been tied to major crypto thefts, and the Bitget connection suggests this crew was active across multiple targets in a short span. The commingling evidence also cut both ways. It helped Chainalysis link the two incidents. But it signals a group confident enough to run proceeds from separate hacks through shared infrastructure, apparently without much fear of the connection being drawn. For stablecoin issuers, the case is a partial win. Their freeze powers helped lock up a large share of the recovered funds. Yet the $325 million conversion into ETH shows exactly where that tool runs out. Once money leaves a freezable asset, the issuer's leverage disappears. Attackers are automating their laundering, as the thousands of recursive transactions show. Investigators are automating their tracing, as Chain is meant to do.

item.content:encoded:
News / Invezz / Evening digest: Nvidia reinstates Huang as CEO, gold rebounds and oil falls

Evening digest: Nvidia reinstates Huang as CEO, gold rebounds and oil falls 3 min read

NVDA XAUUSD UKOIL BTCUSD

Global financial markets saw a broad recovery on Monday after Nvidia announced the immediate reinstatement of Jensen Huang as chief executive, helping revive sentiment towards technology and AI-related assets. Nvidia shares gained 30% in the session, reversing part of last week's steep losses. The chipmaker had plunged 14.01% to $125.53 on Friday, taking its weekly decline to nearly 23%. Its shares had also fallen almost 50% from their October peak. Elsewhere, gold recovered from a more than one-year low, while oil prices declined as traders assessed rising supplies from the Middle East and the reopening of a major Libyan pipeline. Bitcoin also rebounded after falling close to $55,000 over the weekend. Nvidia reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO Nvidia's board unanimously reinstated Jensen Huang as president and chief executive officer with immediate effect, just 10 days after he stepped down from the position. The decision followed several discussions and meetings between Huang and the board. Directors also sought input from senior US government officials before concluding that his return would not pose a national security risk. Board chair Harvey C. Jones said directors remained confident in Huang's leadership. "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers," Jones said. Jones will continue as board chair, while Colette Kress will remain chief financial officer. Kress had assumed the interim CEO position following Huang's departure. Nvidia also established a separate National Security and Export Control Committee comprising independent directors. The committee will oversee trade compliance and assess national security risks. The company is bringing in legal counsel with national security experience and beginning a search for a new chief compliance officer. Nvidia said it would continue cooperating with ongoing government investigations. Gold price rebounds after weekly decline Gold prices recovered on Monday as investors bought the dip following last week's sharp decline. Spot gold climbed 3.9% to $3,639 per ounce, after touching its lowest level since September 2025 on Friday. US gold futures advanced 3.6% to $3,642.50. The recovery followed a decline of more than 9% last week, when an AI-related stock market sell-off prompted some investors to liquidate gold holdings to raise cash and meet margin requirements. Market participants continued to expect a 25-basis-point Federal Reserve rate hike in December, while expectations of a larger 50-basis-point increase had been priced out. Investors are now awaiting Wednesday's October Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) index, the Fed's preferred inflation measure, for further clues on the interest rate outlook. Spot silver gained 6.1% to $43.70 per ounce. Platinum rose 2.9% to $1,336.17, while palladium advanced 0.8% to $901.52. Oil price falls as Libyan pipeline restarts Oil prices dropped nearly 4% on Monday as rising supply expectations and the reopening of Libya's Sharara pipeline weighed on crude markets. Brent crude futures fell 4% to $88.87 a barrel, while US West Texas Intermediate declined 3.98% to $80.09. Libya's National Oil Corporation confirmed that the Sharara pipeline had reopened, with crude beginning to flow into storage tanks at the Akakus facility in Zawiya. JPMorgan expects oil futures to decline towards the high $70s in the first half of 2027, citing an expected supply surplus and increased production from the Middle East and the Americas. However, geopolitical risks continued to limit the downside. Recent attacks involving shipping near the Strait of Hormuz and an alleged Houthi strike on a Saudi refinery raised concerns about potential supply disruptions. Meanwhile, Ukraine's military said it had struck Russia's Lukoil refinery in Perm, damaging three processing units. Russian oil exports from major Baltic and Black Sea terminals were also facing delays due to bad weather and Ukrainian drone attacks. Bitcoin rebounds towards $64,000 before retreating Bitcoin recovered from a weekend low near $55,100, briefly climbing to $64,000 following Nvidia's announcement about Huang's return. The cryptocurrency subsequently surrendered part of its gains and was trading around $61,130 at the time of writing. Veteran trader Dave Weisberger said the weekend decline appeared to represent Bitcoin's third test of a potential price floor this year. He identified heavy trading volume near the lows and a rapid recovery on the weekly chart as possible signs that selling pressure was easing. However, Weisberger cautioned against expecting an immediate V-shaped recovery. "I am not calling for a V bottom," he said. Bloomberg's Mike McGlone offered a different interpretation, suggesting that short sellers buying back their positions had contributed to the rebound. With some Treasury securities offering yields of around 5%, McGlone argued that investors still have reasons to favour bonds over cryptocurrencies. The $60,000-$61,000 range remains an important level to watch. A recovery from that area could establish a higher low, while a break below the weekend low of $55,100 would weaken the argument that Bitcoin has reached a bottom.
